commenti.body:
For a film that’s trying hard to move you, it didn’t succeed at all (for me or Mrs Schools); instead, it felt formulaic, contrived and heavy-handed. (And the less said about that ‘afterlife’ sequence, the better – that felt like a studio note.)

But what’s undeniable is Durkin’s technical prowess as a director. He has an incredible sense of mise en scene and a remarkable compositional eye, a precision to his image making that’s rare and enviable. His first two features are just immaculate as far as I’m concerned
I forgot about the afterlife sequence. That was pretty bad. At least it was framed as a vision that Kevin was having of his brothers. Rather than as something more objective.

Apart from the hokiness of the whole sequence – badly at odds with the rest of the film – it was the fact he had to say, ‘Oh, you must be my older baby brother!’ 

Like, yeah, dude. We know.
I do admit that the movie wasn't perfect, but it definitely made me emotional. Also the afterlife sequence was incredibly kitschy, but that does work for me sometimes. It did here.

The afterlife scene was cringe as it went on and I am glad they didn't end the film there. I really enjoyed the film, not a lot of cuts, most of the frame in the film for was well thought out. Its a sad but hopeful story and I guess the executives wanted some sort of happy scene, but they already had that from the pre-match interviews which brought some appropriate humor into the story, especially the Ric Flair interview.

I thought the film captured the human body in motion absolutely spectacularly.  The wrestling sequences really hammered home the concept of the sport as essentially Ballet with extra testosterone.  Which created such a wonderful contrast with the rest of the film in which the brothers couldn’t express themselves and were constantly stiff and tense under their father’s pressure.   The directing all around was quite top notch, even if I have some minor quibbles with the script.

This film was in development for a while, and I think the family had some objections to where the story was ultimately going. One whole brother was removed from the movie altogether, though he’d been in it for almost three years. It feels like a script that was picked apart and patched back up, appealing more to a certain audience demographic.

I wonder if focus groups didn’t like what could’ve been great gothic horror about generational curses and how the Faustian bargains for success in the entertainment industry play out. That little brother’s death in real life was gruesome and literally haunted the family. He was electrocuted and drowned in a puddle in Canada when the father was just beginning his career as a wrestling heel. They also didn’t mention he dressed up as a Nazi in the ring. There was another brother Chris who committed suicide at 21 when he was pushed into wrestling but wasn’t good at it because of poor health. 

I think they ultimately decided on  a “we’re just fun loving country folk from Texas who had our faith tested” drama instead of committing to horror. So, they threw that scene in to explain why they were talking about curses. That’s the only explanation why Kevin pulls back from the family. I think it was because the story shifted genres.

Some good soundtrack choices, too. My complaint with a lot of features these days is directors jump from writer-director too fast and writers work in tv too much and don’t understand how to pace a feature. The result is a choppy film with some great scenes but that feels distracted overall. This especially shows with musical choices. They want a certain song to do the storytelling for them and it becomes quite literal. 

Example, the reunion on the lake scene. They really wanted Blue Oyster Cult in the film for that scene delivering the payoff, and it fell flat. If the movie was horror, it would’ve worked out because you see the brothers all reunited in the prime of their lives and the choice Kevin has. He has a family of his own having escaped his abusive childhood. 

But they didn’t do that. The wrestling scenes were incredible, though. Love the Ric Flair fight. And I love when Kevin walks into the ring to Rush. This feels like a genuine music choice, like the family were fans and worked out to it and got pumped listening to it. I hate that we always hear the same music from certain periods, especially the early to mid 70s.

I LOVED the afterlife sequence!

I think if it was done by any other director, it would’ve been corny but I thought it was incredibly moving.

One of the comments here called this “trying hard to move you” and I couldn’t disagree more. I was actually surprised by how subdued this film was in portraying BIG emotions despite the extremely tragic story it portrays. I expected weeping every 2-3 seconds but the film chooses not to exploit it. 

Like almost to the point that when there is an emotional scene, like when Kevin finds Kerry’s body, omg it hit like a big yellow school bus. Zac Efron was amazing here and esp in the final button of the sequence when he laments that he “used to be a brother” BOI!!! Forget about it. 

I don’t think this is a perfect film. It skips over a whole Von Erich brother and the pacing needs to be much tighter. But it’s such an emotionally devastating look at toxic masculinity.

See, this sounds very plausible. 

And it also recalls a tendency in Durkin’s last film as well – a tentative quality to the storytelling that’s at odds with the precision of the filmmaking. Specifically, a reluctance to commit to the genre it’s hinting at. The only problem with ‘The Nest’, for me, is that it refuses to become the ghost story it’s constantly promising to be.

Maybe he’s pitching horror because producers are willing to take risks on newer directors since the audience is loyal and these films usually exceed their budget at the box office. A24 looks like they’re trying to get away from horror, though, and they had a good draw with the cast and source material. Too bad, because this movie could’ve been much better, and it’s the script that held it back.

Kerry Von Erich used to enter his matches to Tom Sawyer, so the Rush choice is actually kind of historically accurate, although his brother Kevin actually entered the ring to Stranglehold by Ted Nugent

Yeah the ending with him crying was beautifully executed symbolism. I’m not sure how people are saying it was “trying hard to be emotional” when for me it was just straight up was gut wrenching.

Great writing and great performances will typically invest you into the emotion of the story which the Iron Claw succeeds fully in imo

I appreciate the after life choice. I think people misread it as coming from Kerry, when it’s from Kevin. I’d imagine if you lost all of your siblings you’d at least hope in whatever world came after, for most it’s a visual description of dreams come true land, you’d  want them to be together because you can’t be.
Yeah, I agree fully. Some of the techniques on show told the story beautifully. Particularly the slow zooms you mentioned. Really impressive and really feels of the era in which it's set. Loved it.
